# The Version Control Landscape

After this page you can say what version control is for, why Git is the usual tool, and what a forge is.

## Why you need a history

Without version control, a desk project grows copies:

```text
desk-api/
├── app.py
├── app_backup.py
├── app_final.py
├── app_final_v2.py
└── app_really_final_fixed.py
```

You lose which file is current, who changed the login line, and any way to undo Tuesday without also undoing Wednesday. Two people editing `app.py` overwrite each other.

A **version control system** (VCS) keeps one tree of files, a history of snapshots, and a way to merge parallel work.

## Three generations

| Generation | Idea | Examples |
|------------|------|----------|
| Local | History on one disk | SCCS, RCS |
| Centralized | One server is the repository | CVS, Subversion, Perforce |
| Distributed | Every clone is a full repository | Git, Mercurial |

**Local** tools recorded deltas next to the files. Fine for one person on one machine.

**Centralized** tools put the real history on a server. You check out a working copy. Committing needs the network. If the server dies, history you do not have locally is gone.

**Distributed** tools give every clone the whole history. `git commit` is a local operation. A **remote** is another copy you push to when you choose. That is why Git works on a train, and why rewriting commits you already shared is a people problem.

## Why Git

Git won the ecosystem. The properties that matter for this book:

- A commit is a **snapshot** of the whole tree, not a pile of patches as the primary model.
- A **branch** is a cheap name for one commit. Merging and rebasing are graph operations.
- Object names are **hashes** of content. Bit flips show up as missing or mismatched objects.
- Log, diff, commit, branch, and merge all work without a network.
- Hosting platforms speak Git remotes. Learning Git is not loyalty to one website.

Git vs Subversion, the comparison that still comes up:

| | Git | Subversion |
|--|-----|------------|
| Architecture | Distributed | Centralized |
| Offline commit | Yes | No |
| Branch | A name on a commit | A copy in the tree |
| Typical remote | Any number | One canonical server |

Mercurial is also distributed. Git is what forges, CI systems, and GitOps engines speak.

## What a forge is

A **repository** is a directory Git is tracking (the `.git` folder plus your files).

A **forge** is a Git hosting platform: the website and services around repositories. Issues, pull requests, CI, packages, and user accounts live on the forge. GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, Bitbucket, Gerrit, and SourceHut are forges. This book treats Git first, then the platforms.

Git is the tool. The forge is the product you log into. GitOps (later) is the idea that the same Git history should drive what runs in production.

## What Git is not

- Not a backup by itself. A single laptop clone can die; you still need remotes and backups.
- Not a file-sync tool. Dropbox overwrites. Git records snapshots and asks you to merge.
- Not GitHub. You can use Git for years with a forge you run yourself, or with no forge at all.
